Nvidia, CEO Jensen Huang sued over disclosures related to suspected Chinese spy

Jensen Huang, president and CEO of Nvidia, waits for a groundbreaking ceremony for an expansion of Coherent's manufacturing facility to begin on Jun 16, 2026, in Sherman, Texas. (File photo: AP/Jeffrey McWhorter)

FAST

Nvidia and chief executive Jensen Huang were sued on Monday (Nov 9) in a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties with a suspected Chinese spy. According to a complaint filed in federal court in San Jose, California, the defendants misled shareholders about Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him, and did not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. The New York Times reported last month about the alleged relationship, and that US authorities had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Jensen Huang told Nvidia's employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the alleged relationship. He co-founded Nvidia, and has led the Santa Clara, California-based company as it became the world's most valuable chipmaker and made him one of the world's most prominent symbols of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia announced a probe into the matter on Sunday. Its shares closed down 4.3 per cent on Monday, reducing Nvidia's market capitalisation by approximately US$190 billion. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after the US stock market closed. It is common for shareholders to sue companies after unexpected share price declines. Nvidia shareholders led by Mark Kistenmacher are seeking unspecified damages from the defendants.

Nov 9 : Tom Brady has ended his three-year involvement as a minority investor in Birmingham City, the English second-tier club said on Monday, thanking the seven-times Super Bowl champion for his support. "Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the Club over the last three years," the Championship side said in a statement. "It was truly amazing to have someone with Tom's experience and passion associated with the Club, and the Club looks forward to continuing to build on that foundation from the training ground to the Birmingham community." The club gave no reason for Brady's departure and did not specify what would happen to his stake.

Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week

Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass but conviction appears unlikely.

FAST

WASHINGTON: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war. William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress. US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday (Nov 9), setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power. Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.

"They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment," he told a press conference. Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with President Donald Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats. US President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military's performance in Iran and Venezuela: "Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him." House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see”. Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections , intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as “courageous and historic”. Accused of taking huge kickbacks, Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, “burst into tears”. The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of the required two-thirds majority. By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight. HEGSETH SAYS HE IS NOT WORRIED Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: "It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me." Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: "We're not worried about that." He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push "unfair," telling reporters: "I think Pete's done a good job. I really do."

Related:

Trump revives election fraud claims after crushing midterm defeat

Republicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing

Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth's performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where the US military deposed that country's president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital. "Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, where we fought forever and nothing happened?" Trump asked. DEFENCE SPENDING AT RISK? Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package. Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," Massie said. Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a "hard yes" on a measure to impeach Hegseth. US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial. "Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting," he said. Massie's articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanours" ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was "punishable by DEATH!"

item.title: He transformed Africa’s biggest airline. Can he turn around SIA-backed Air India?
item.description: Tewolde Gebremariam’s success with Ethiopian Airlines could help revive Air India, but analysts warn that fierce competition, mounting costs and operational challenges will make his job far from easy.
item.dc:creator: Collin Furtado

Asia

He transformed Africa’s biggest airline. Can he turn around SIA-backed Air India?

Tewolde Gebremariam’s success with Ethiopian Airlines could help revive Air India, but analysts warn that fierce competition, mounting costs and operational challenges will make his job far from easy.

Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam attends an aviation event in New Delhi, India, Nov 3, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Bhawika Chhabra)

FAST

SINGAPORE: Turning around an airline that has  struggled to make money for nearly two decades is no small feat. But the man now tasked with  reviving Air India has built an aviation powerhouse before - and he is impatient to do it again.

In his first major public appearance since his appointment in August, Air India CEO Tewolde Gebremariam outlined plans to turn around the loss-making carrier, saying he expects it to return to profitability “very soon”.

“I am more impatient than the shareholders to see profitability,” Gebremariam told attendees at an aviation conference in New Delhi on Tuesday (Nov 3) - although he offered no timeline for achieving that goal.

His ambitions are sweeping: Expand the airline’s international network, acquire more long-haul aircraft and develop major aviation hubs across India while cutting costs. The stakes also extend beyond India.

Singapore Airlines (SIA) owns a 25.1 per cent stake in the carrier, an investment that has come under scrutiny as Air India's losses mount and its owners face calls to inject more capital.

Related:

CNA Explains: Why is SIA staying invested in loss-making Air India, and can its long-term bet pay off?

Beyond Air India’s losses: Why Indian airlines are struggling more than others, and sounding the alarm

Gebremariam, however, has a track record of building an aviation powerhouse. During his 11 years at the helm of Ethiopian Airlines, revenue grew more than fourfold as the carrier expanded its fleet and international reach.

But analysts say there is a crucial difference between his previous assignment and the one he has taken on now.

Ethiopian Airlines was already profitable when Gebremariam became CEO in 2011.

Air India, by contrast, is grappling with mounting losses, fierce competition and operational constraints. Analysts say his experience could help revive the struggling Indian carrier, but caution that the strategies that worked in Africa may not necessarily deliver the same results in India. “The two tenures are not comparable in challenges,” said Ameya Joshi, founder of aviation analytics website Network Thoughts.

“Strategies cannot be copy-pasted as such.” TRANSFORMING ETHIOPIAN AIRLINES Under Gebremariam’s tenure, Ethiopian Airlines grew into Africa’s largest carrier - with annual revenue surging from about US$1 billion in 2011 to US$4.5 billion by the time he stepped down in 2022.

Its fleet rose from just 33 aircraft to 130, with annual passenger numbers also quadrupling to 12 million, as the airline expanded its international network and cemented the capital Addis Ababa’s position as a major aviation hub.

Ethiopian Airlines former CEO, Tewolde Gebremariam, during an interview with AFP in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Apr 21, 2020. (Photo: AFP/Michael Tewelde)

Mark D Martin, founder and CEO of aviation consultancy Martin Consulting, attributed much of that success to Gebremariam’s grasp of airline finances and emphasis on operational efficiency over branding. “His two pillars are maintenance and flight service,” Martin said - pointing to Gebremariam's focus on flight crew procedures, aircraft upkeep and passenger experience.

Ethiopian Airlines was already profitable when Gebremariam's took over from his  predecessor Girma Wake  in January 2011 .

His achievement was in scaling up an established, financially healthy airline rather than rescuing one in distress.

Mayur Patel, an aviation analyst at aviation data firm OAG, said the struggles of other African national carriers created an opportunity for Ethiopian Airlines to establish Ethiopia’s capital Addis Ababa as a major aviation hub - connecting the continent with the rest of the world.

The airline capitalised on that by establishing an extensive international network and making transit more convenient for passengers travelling through Addis Ababa.

Martin shared his own positive experience flying with the airline from Delhi  to Vienna via Addis Ababa earlier this year , which provided hotel accommodation, meals and airport transfers during an  11-hour layover. “It's like what travel was back in the 50s and 60s, where the airline also gave you hotel and transports during a layover,” he said.

But conditions now are fundamentally different for Air India in the current landscape, Martin said.

Gebremariam is “inheriting probably the toughest challenge that he can ever take up,” he added. CAN GEBREMARIAM’S ETHIOPIAN AIRLINES PLAYBOOK WORK IN INDIA?  Gebremariam’s strategy for Air India bears some resemblance to the approach that helped Ethiopian Airlines become an African aviation powerhouse: Expand international operations, strengthen transit hubs and keep costs under control.

His plans include acquiring more wide-body aircraft, opening up international routes and developing major Indian airports into hubs connecting passengers to destinations around the world.

An Air India Airbus A350 aeroplane is displayed at Wings India 2024 aviation at Begumpet airport, Hyderabad, India, Jan 18, 2024. (Photo: Reuters/Almaas Masood)

Analysts broadly support these ambitions, but warn that executing them will require substantial investment, time and a competitive edge in an already crowded market.

A key part of Gebremariam’s strategy hinges on expanding Air India's fleet of wide-body aircraft, which can carry more passengers over longer distances.

Ameya Joshi, founder of aviation analytics website Network Thoughts, said the airline needs more such aircraft to grow its international operations. But additional orders will require fresh capital and approval from investors, he added.

Deliveries could also take years, he cautioned, by which time market conditions may have changed.

And even with more aircraft, profitability would depend on Air India's ability to attract enough passengers to fill the additional seats.

Funding is already proving to be a pressing issue.

Reuters reported in August that Air India was seeking about US$1.5 billion in fresh equity from its owners, Tata Group and SIA.

In September, Tata approved a US$1.1 billion capital infusion, representing its share of the proposed funding, while SIA announced that it was seeking stronger governance rights before committing more capital.

Beyond securing aircraft and funding, Gebremariam must also decide where Air India can compete most effectively.

Martin said the airline’s focus on international expansion was a step in the right direction and believes it should prioritise long-haul routes to destinations in Europe and the United States, where it could generate more foreign-currency revenue.

But building a competitive international network will require more than additional flights, Martin said.

He warned that the lack of dedicated airline hub facilities at Indian airports could hamper Air India’s ambitions. Such facilities allow airlines to consolidate operations within a terminal, making transfers between connecting flights more seamless.

Closer cooperation with airport operators would therefore be crucial, he said.

Air India’s international ambitions also face an obstacle largely beyond Gebremariam’s control: Pakistan’s airspace restrictions on Indian carriers, which have been in place since April 2025.

The restrictions have forced Indian airlines to take longer routes on several westbound flights to Europe and North America, pushing up fuel consumption and operating costs. Together, Europe and North America accounted for more than a quarter of India's outbound international passenger traffic in 2024, or about 10.7 million passengers, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA).

With westbound operations becoming more expensive, Patel said eastbound markets such as Southeast Asia and Australia have become more attractive for Air India's expansion.

Against this backdrop, Gebremariam has said the airline is exploring Bengaluru as a third hub alongside Delhi and Mumbai, as part of efforts to reshape its international network.

Bengaluru could play an important role in connecting domestic passengers to international flights, said Patel - although developing such a network would take time.

A ground staff member looks on as an Air India aircraft takes off at Kempegowda International Airport in Bengaluru on Jun 10, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Idrees Mohammed)

Joshi noted that Air India already has an established hub in Delhi, which has long supported domestic and international connections. With more aircraft, competitive fares and an improved passenger experience, the airline could build on that foundation, he added.

Both analysts pointed to India's vast domestic passenger market as a potential advantage.

Rather than relying solely on attracting international transit passengers away from established hubs such as Dubai and Singapore, Air India could draw on domestic demand to fill its long-haul flights.

That could give Gebremariam a valuable starting point as he attempts to build a more competitive international airline - even if replicating his Ethiopian Airlines success proves far from straightforward. AIR INDIA’S TOUGHEST CHALLENGE AHEAD For all his ambitions to expand Air India's international reach, Gebremariam faces a more immediate challenge: Stemming the airline’s mounting losses while grappling with a host of operational and safety concerns.

Air India and its budget subsidiary Air India Express reported combined losses of about US$2.33 billion in the financial year ended March 2026, more than double the previous year's losses. The carrier is also dealing with the aftermath of the June 2025 crash of Flight AI171 in Ahmedabad, which killed 260 people and intensified scrutiny of its safety standards. India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has yet to release its final report on the cause of the crash.

Wreckage of the Air India Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner plane outside Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport, in Ahmedabad, India, on Jul 12, 2025. (Photo: Reuters/Amit Dave)

Martin said Gebremariam had inherited an exceptionally difficult assignment, including managing the fallout from the disaster and developments arising from the ongoing investigation. Beyond the crashes, the airline is also contending with challenges like higher fuel costs, delays in refurbishing its aircraft and regulatory scrutiny over safety and compliance lapses, according to reports.

The airline also faces fierce competition from domestic market leader IndiGo and established international carriers, making it harder to raise fares to offset rising expenses.

Patel said India's highly price-sensitive market leaves airlines with little room to pass rising costs onto passengers without affecting demand.

He added that fuel expenses and longer flight routes caused by Pakistan's airspace restrictions also continue to weigh heavily on the airline.

Given these challenges, Gebremariam's immediate priority should be to reduce losses rather than push for a swift return to profitability.

The new CEO has already moved to tighten spending. Air India has set up a dedicated team to identify cost savings and introduced stricter spending approvals, according to an internal memo reported by Reuters in October. Bloomberg reported in September that Gebremariam was also considering merging Air India with its budget subsidiary, Air India Express, to streamline operations and reduce costs. Martin supported the idea, saying a merger could eliminate overlapping functions and improve efficiency. Patel said the airline's tighter approach to spending was already evident in its dealings with suppliers, with expenditure coming under greater scrutiny. But he questioned how much further costs could be cut, particularly when major expenses such as fuel remain largely beyond the airline's control. Ultimately, even a successful cost-cutting drive may not deliver the quick turnaround Gebremariam is seeking. Martin believes the former Ethiopian Airlines chief has the experience and strategy needed to restore Air India to profitability, but estimates that the process could take three to five years. “I think we need to be a little more patient,” he said.

Commentary: Jensen Huang Is bigger than Nvidia – and it’s a problem

The revelation of the CEO’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not just shaking up the chipmaker but the entire AI world, says Shuli Ren for Bloomberg Opinion.

FAST

HONG KONG: When a high-profile chief executive is in trouble, investors worry about key-person risk and whether the company will continue to prosper. But what if that businessman is crucial to an entire narrative that has underpinned the global markets boom?  Nvidia said on Sunday (Nov 8) that it was opening an investigation into Jensen Huang , after the CEO acknowledged that he had a romantic relationship with a business executive whom US intelligence determined was a Chinese spy .  The path forward – and Huang’s future – will depend on what emerges from the board’s fact-finding process. But the revelation itself is shaking up the entire artificial intelligence world.  WILL NVIDIA’S MONEY KEEP FLOWING IN THE SECTOR? Nvidia is not only the sector’s most valuable publicly listed company, with a market cap of US$4.5 trillion, but has lent its own creditworthiness to speed up infrastructure growth.

Over the last three years, it has offered US$300 billion in financial support to customers, in addition to investing billions into startups including neoclouds, or data centre operators that lease out computing power to AI labs.  Despite having only a 3.4 per cent stake, Huang is very much the boss and the architect of Nvidia’s corporate strategies. He has no heir apparent and has created an informal organisation structure whereby his direct reports – as many as 60, according to Bernstein Research – are tasked with rapidly implementing his decisions.  Will Nvidia’s money keep on flowing now that the central banker of AI is in a bit of trouble himself?  BAD TIMING FOR DATA CENTRES This is bad timing for neoclouds. As the likes of CoreWeave are hit with skyrocketing borrowing costs and financing channels close, they naturally look to Nvidia for a lifeline.  Australia’s Firmus Grid, for instance, is reportedly in talks with the company for follow-on venture investments after pulling a much-anticipated initial public offering in Sydney. Deal negotiations may well be put on hold or scrapped altogether.

Related:

Commentary: Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights growing risks for us all

Commentary: Who’s paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom

With Huang’s authority challenged, it’s only natural that Nvidia’s dealmakers take a more defensive stance and step back from vendor financing to customers, which has already worsened the chipmaker’s credit profile.  The cost of protecting Nvidia’s debt against default has tripled this year, as investors look to hedge against potential losses from mounting debt tied to data centres. Its corporate bond spread has widened as well.  STAR POWER TARNISHED And how about AI infrastructure developments across Asia? The worry is that Nvidia will have to slow down shipments to the region while the company is under public scrutiny.  The Chinese woman who Huang had an affair with was an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which has been building data centres in Southeast Asia. The operator reportedly rented compute to Alibaba Group and gave China a backdoor way of getting access to advanced Nvidia chips.

This screengrab from video footage by CTI obtained via AFPTV on Nov 9, 2026 shows Alice Huang (right), a Chinese executive linked to the data centre company called Megaspeed, attending a dinner hosted by Nvidia's chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang (left) at a restaurant in Taipei on May 22, 2025, during Computex, the island's top tech expo. (Image: AFPTV/CTI via AFP) AFPTV / CTI / AFP

As such, national security risks will surface just as Asian banks are getting more comfortable with chip financing and capital deployments into data centres are gaining momentum.  Going forward, the pace of billion-dollar deals could slow as lenders not only question how fast graphics processing units, or GPUs, will become technologically obsolete, but also whom their ultimate customers are. A charismatic salesman, Huang has done a lot of talking, predicting the next trillion-dollar company and promoting Asia’s ecosystem. With his star power tarnished however, the AI trade is looking increasingly shaky. A bear market is looming.

Source: Bloomberg/ch

Nov 9 : Trump Media & Technology Group swung to a third-quarter profit on Monday, while its revenue more than tripled from a year earlier, fueled by growth in its Truth API data-licensing business. Shares of the company rose about 1 per cent in extended trading. Founded by US President Donald Trump and known for its Truth Social platform, Trump Media & Technology Group has increasingly sought to transform itself from a social media company into a broader technology and investment business. The company, which is in the process of merging with TAE Technologies in a pivot toward fusion energy, reiterated that the $6-billion deal would close in the current quarter.

Earlier this year, Trump Media launched Truth API, describing it as a subscription-based data feed that provides licensed, low-latency access to publicly available Truth Social posts. Truth API and the Truth+ streaming platform together added $1.8 million in subscription revenue, accounting for the bulk of the company's revenue growth. Revenue soared 205 per cent to $3.0 million in the quarter ended September 30. Last month, Reuters reported that Truth Social has signed Bloomberg, Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading as customers, with subscribers paying between $60,000 and $100,000 a month for faster access to Truth Social posts. Trump Media shares have fallen nearly 70 per cent this year, including a roughly 32 per cent decline since Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, results widely seen as a rebuke of Trump's policies. "While the market was trading on headlines, the underlying business didn't flinch," interim CEO Kevin McGurn said on a post-earnings call. "Our balance sheet didn't change from Tuesday to Wednesday. Our product traction didn't reverse." The company recorded $409.7 million in net income, driven largely by gains on its cryptocurrency holdings and related securities. This compared to a net loss of $54.8 million a year earlier.

Nov 9 : Switzerland's Granit Xhaka will miss his side's final two Nations League Group B1 games with Slovenia and Scotland after suffering a calf injury, the Swiss FA announced on Monday.  The 34-year-old midfielder had been restored to Murat Yakin's squad after missing the October clashes with Scotland, Slovenia and North Macedonia after admitting to obtaining a forged COVID-19 vaccination certificate in 2022.  However, the Swiss team said that Xhaka, who has played 152 times for his country, had been injured and would not feature in the upcoming games against Slovenia in Maribor on Friday and at home to Scotland in St. Gallen on Monday.  "Granit Xhaka has to withdraw from the Swiss national team camp due to a calf injury," a team statement said.

Nov 9 : SpaceX is planning a roughly $24 billion gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility in Starbase, Texas, according to a public hearing notice. The rockets-to-AI company's request comes as opposition to data centers grows, with voters rejecting them in 40 of 41 local ballot measures and Democrats, some of whom had campaigned on pausing new projects, taking control of the US Congress and the Texas governor's office in the midterm elections. The filing shows SpaceX, which bought Elon Musk's AI lab xAI earlier this year, has applied for a property tax abatement for the project. The Starbase City Commission will consider the abatement, plus a related economic development agreement, at a public meeting on December 9. The notice describes $24 billion as the estimated capital investment for the project's initial phases. It said the work may be done in multiple phases and could include future expansions.

SpaceX would construct, own and operate the facilities. The project would be among the largest private investments in the Rio Grande Valley. Building its own power plant could let SpaceX skip a years-long wait to plug a project into Texas' main power grid. The notice did not say how large the abatement would be or how long it would last. It also gave no details on the plant's generating capacity or the scale of the computing operation. SpaceX affiliate Lone Star Mineral Development has filed plans for an 8-mile natural gas pipeline to Starbase, called Starpipe, that is scheduled for service by January 2027. It will feed a planned plant to turn the gas into liquid methane for Starship rockets, according to filings Reuters reviewed in June. The company last month reported a 161 per cent jump in revenue and a ninefold increase in AI revenue for its third quarter. The company has been renting out computing capacity to Google, Anthropic and others. Bloomberg News first reported on the development.
